title: Federal Judge Blocks Trump Rule Capping Foreign Student, Journalist Visa Stays
excerpt: A Boston federal judge froze a DHS rule that would have replaced the decades-old ‘duration of status’ system with four-year caps for students and 240-day caps for journalists, one day before it was set to take effect.
body:
• U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor in Boston issued a preliminary injunction on Monday, blocking the DHS rule one day before it was scheduled to take effect on Tuesday.
  • The rule, finalized in July, would have capped F student and J exchange-visitor visas at four years and I journalist visas at 240 days, ending the nearly 50-year-old "duration of status" system.
  • Saylor found the government's national-security and fraud-prevention justifications "exceptionally weak" and warned the rule could inflict "catastrophic" damage on U.S. higher education and the economy.
  • Roughly 1.6 million people hold F visas and 500,000 hold J visas; a further hearing is scheduled for Oct. 2 as the case continues.

What happened

A federal judge in Boston on Monday blocked the Trump administration from imposing strict new time limits on how long foreign students and journalists may remain in the United States, dealing a last-minute legal defeat to one of the administration's central immigration policies.

U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor granted a preliminary injunction sought by a coalition of unions and higher-education advocacy groups, ruling just one day before the Department of Homeland Security rule was set to take effect on Tuesday, according to Reuters.

Saylor said the department had adopted the policy on "exceptionally weak" rationales. The agency cited national security and the need to prevent fraud in the visa program, but the judge found it had neither engaged with the concerns raised about the change nor considered less burdensome alternatives. The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Context and background

For nearly five decades, the United States has admitted foreign students under a "duration of status" system that lets them stay for as long as their academic program requires. Saylor noted the system has permitted tens of millions of foreign students and researchers to come to the country, driving "groundbreaking research in science, medicine, and technology, substantial economic growth, and a host of other benefits, often on a vast scale."

The rule adopted by DHS in July would have replaced that system with fixed admission periods: F visas for international students and J visas for cultural exchange visitors would have been capped at four years, with a 30-day departure window and extensions routed through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. I visas for foreign journalists, which can currently last years, would have been cut to 240 days at a time, with Chinese journalists limited to 90 days.

The legal challenge was filed on Aug. 18 by NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the American Federation of Teachers, United Auto Workers Local 2322, and The NewsGuild-CWA, among others, which argued the rule was procedurally flawed and would cause irreparable harm.

"The damage to the higher education system and to the economy of the United States is likely to be catastrophic."

— Judge F. Dennis Saylor, U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

Impact and analysis

The scale of the affected population is enormous. About 1.6 million people currently hold F visas and another 500,000 hold J visas, according to the court. Saylor noted that major research universities such as MIT and Harvard enroll large shares of foreign students, particularly at the graduate level, and would likely face hundreds of millions of dollars in costs along with declining enrollment if the rule took effect.

The judge also flagged a distinct danger for foreign journalists. Because extensions would have been granted at DHS officials' discretion with no appeals process, he suggested the system could target members of the press critical of the government — and that the rule's real purpose might be control over academia and the media.

The diaspora angle

For Indian students — one of the largest national cohorts on American campuses and among the biggest beneficiaries of the duration-of-status system — the injunction preserves a regime that graduate and doctoral programs depend on. PhD programs routinely run longer than four years, and the fixed caps would have forced thousands of students into uncertain extension battles mid-degree. "While the case continues, this relief preserves the longstanding system that enables our colleges and universities — and our country — to attract, educate, and retain global talent," Miriam Feldblum, head of the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said of the ruling.

What to watch next

Saylor's order pauses enforcement without deciding the merits; a further hearing is set for Oct. 2. Until the litigation resolves, the decades-old duration-of-status framework stays in place.
nri_angle: The injunction preserves the duration-of-status system that Indian students — one of the largest cohorts on U.S. campuses — depend on, sparing doctoral and other long programs from forced extension battles under four-year caps.
